sections.html:
The recorder's main line is (330) 297-3553, with a fax at (330) 297-7349 and the same number for copy requests. Copy requests can also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM. Call before you drive a deed over to confirm counter hours.

Ravenna is the county seat, and the auditor's forms use 449 South Meridian Street as the county's address for property work. Whether you hand-carry or mail a deed, it goes to the auditor on that street first, because the transfer there comes before recording.

Staff do not run searches for you. They will point you to the indexes and help you read them, and anyone studying title or family history is welcome to use the office.

sections.h2: What the recorder keeps on file
sections.html:
The office keeps a permanent record of every paper that moves or burdens land in the county. Each filing gets a time stamp and a document number, then goes to microfilm and image storage and into the computer index.

  • Deeds, mortgages and easements.
  • Land titles and rights-of-way.
  • Federal tax liens and unemployment liens.
  • Uniform Commercial Code filings.
  • Leases of several kinds, along with military discharges and records of military burials.

Fees collected here are split between the county general fund and the state housing trust fund. For a seller, the point is that mortgage and lien releases appear in these same indexes, where the buyer's title examiner will look.

The county follows the state schedule and adds one warning: a paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up an added $20.00. The dollar figures below come from R.C. 317.32.

  • Pages one and two together: $34, split evenly between base and trust fund shares.
  • Every page after that: $8, again split evenly.
  • A county-set preservation surcharge, capped at $5 and paid to the general fund.
  • Certified copies: $2 per page in total.
  • Each marginal reference in a separate instrument: $4 in total.

The surcharge can be anything up to the cap, so ask the recorder for the total on your exact document. The statute counts the caption page, and any fraction of a page counts as a page.

sections.h2: What the auditor takes before a deed is recorded
sections.html:
The auditor's side comes first. The real estate department transfers deeds and similar papers ahead of recording. The conveyance charge is four dollars for each $1,000 of price, plus fifty cents for every parcel moved. The DTE 100 form, Conveyance of Real Property, travels with the deed.

A county board may also adopt a transfer tax on grantors of no more than 30 cents on each $100 of value, collected by the auditor ahead of recording (R.C. 322.02). Ask the auditor whether Portage County has one in force.

The auditor's pages also offer parcel ownership histories, valuations, sales information and tax data, which are worth printing before you meet a buyer.

Three desks handle most of a sale.

Portage County offices involved in a home sale
OfficeTask in a saleWhat to know
RecorderRecords the deed, mortgage and releasesMain (330) 297-3553; fax (330) 297-7349; online index called Find My Deed
AuditorTransfers the deed, sets the conveyance fee$4.00 per $1,000 plus 50 cents per parcel; DTE 100 form
TreasurerBills and collects property taxTwo bills a year, about half in February and half in July

The deed does not settle unpaid tax, so get a payoff for the parcel from the treasurer, and have the title company say who bears the half now accruing.

The recorder links a "Find My Deed" search, and the county posts scanned lease books on its site, with books numbered 92 through 114 posted so far and more promised as scanning continues. Indexes default to one page for some older volumes and pages, so a document shown as a single page may run longer. Call or email the office for correct page totals before you order copies.

Copies of all records are available on request. Bring a parcel number or the names on the deed, since staff will not search on your behalf. The auditor's property search gives the owner history and sales for a parcel, which narrows what to ask for.

Ohio also requires a conveyance to be prepared and signed under the Revised Code before it is accepted for record.

sections.h2: What to have ready before you record
sections.html:
Bring a deed that was prepared and signed under the Ohio Revised Code. Have the auditor's transfer done first, and keep the DTE 100 form with the paperwork.

  • The signed, acknowledged deed with the marginal rule observed.
  • Payment for the auditor's conveyance fee and the recorder's fees.
  • A parcel number, so staff and the online index can match the right record.

After acceptance the office stamps the time, numbers the document, films and scans it, and adds it to the index. After closing, request a copy of the recorded deed for your own file.

sections.h2: From closing table to recorded deed
sections.html:
Here is how a Portage County deed travels after you sign it.

  1. The deed is prepared and signed under the Ohio Revised Code, with the margins left clear.
  2. It goes first to the auditor's real estate department at 449 South Meridian Street, along with the DTE 100 form and the conveyance charge.
  3. The auditor completes the transfer and collects any grantor transfer tax that applies.
  4. The recorder accepts the deed, stamps the time, numbers it, films and scans it and adds it to the index.
  5. Your lender records the mortgage satisfaction after payoff, and it shows up in the same index.

If you are using a title company, it usually walks the deed through each step. If you are doing it yourself, call the recorder at (330) 297-3553 for the total on your document and the auditor for the transfer charge, and bring a payment method for each office. Once recording is done, ask for a copy of the recorded deed so you have it for your own file, and ask for the page count in advance if the document is an older one.

The county covers 504 square miles of Northeast Ohio, had 161,791 residents in 2020, and 31.1% of occupied homes are rented.

  • Format the deed to Ohio's page and margin rules to avoid the $20 surcharge.
  • Record a mortgage satisfaction soon after payoff, so the buyer's title search is clean.
  • Visit the auditor for the transfer step before the recorder.

The recorder's office has also run a Good Deeds Program, meant to help owners prepare now and avoid the probate court process later. Ask the office for current dates and locations if a family property may pass to heirs.

A house with liens, back taxes or a stalled estate can still be sold for cash, and the buyer's closing agent handles the filings.

faqs.q: What is the recorder's phone number?
faqs.a: The main line is (330) 297-3553, and the fax is (330) 297-7349. Copy requests use the same phone number and also go by email to PCREC.COPIES@PORTAGECO.COM.

faqs.q: How much does the auditor charge to transfer a deed?
faqs.a: Four dollars per $1,000 of the price plus fifty cents a parcel. The recorder's fee is separate, and the auditor's transfer happens first.

faqs.q: Is there an extra recording fee?
faqs.a: Yes, in one case. A paper that breaks the state marginal rule picks up $20.00 on top of the usual charges, so check margins before you submit.

faqs.q: Can I look up a deed online?
faqs.a: Yes. The recorder links a Find My Deed search, and the auditor's real estate site shows ownership history and sales. Page counts on older volumes can be wrong, so confirm them by phone.

faqs.q: Does the recorder pay off my mortgage or my taxes?
faqs.a: No. The recorder files papers and nothing more. Payoffs run through your lender and the county treasurer, and a closing agent normally arranges both.
